claims: Yadav's1978study treats carts as working rural transport and distinguishes multiple designs rather than one universal form.
The loading discussion connects platform height with effort of loading above it and clearance for carrying logs beneath; figure3shows a log suspended below the frame and a load above.
Wheel diameter,rim width,ground contact and load interact in the paper's account of sinkage and resistance. Hub/axle friction,wear and bearing cost are also considered.
The concluding discussion treats affordable local materials and available village artisans as constraints on practical improvement.
limits: Historical engineering account, not current prevalence, a validated modern construction plan or a named wheelmaker's testimony.
The source distinguishes bullock carts from manually operated two-wheel carts; do not silently merge them.
Exclude its dated health claim, formulas, recommended dimensions,load limits and prices as present guidance.
Table1uses Agricultural Census1970–71 and Statistical Abstract1973 with historical district boundaries. Avoid importing totals into a current Odisha claim.
Fig3is an observed photograph in a study, not evidence of a uniform local practice or an instructed safe loading method. Do not reproduce source figures without cleared rights.

draft_guidance: Keep a compact historical design essay. Begin with the cart as a working object and the relationship of wheel,load androad. Use one memorable loading example from1978 and the practical limits of cost/materials/repair. Avoid broad nostalgia,extinction,antiquity,modern transport recommendations or a manufactured workshop scene. Three or four source notes only if each source performs a useful job; NMMA is optional.
